articles.title: Sylvester Stallone Says Daughter’s ‘Tulsa King’ Casting is ‘Of Course’ Nepotism: ‘Obviously We Let Them Have Every Advantage’
articles.summary: Sylvester Stallone has heard the nepotism allegations, and frankly, he doesn’t care. Stallone’s real-life daughter, Scarlet Rose Stallone, co-stars with him as Spencer in “Tulsa King,” and takes on a larger role in the family business and on-screen for Season 4.
body: While his career may have helped his daughter land the role, he says she still has to prove herself.

“Can they maintain that level of excellence? That’s out of our hands,” he said. “But if you can open the door, we’ll see if they have the ability to go through it. It might be a question of, ‘Now how do I get out of this?’ Be careful what you wish for.”

In “Tulsa King,” Stallone plays mob boss Dwight “The General” Manfredi, who is exiled to Tulsa, Oklahoma, after serving 25 years in prison. After their Season 1 introduction, Stallone’s daughter returns in Season 4 as a former barista turned horse caretaker and stablehand at Fennario Ranch (hired by Manfredi).
Season 4 of the Paramount+ series “Tulsa King” premiered on Oct. 16, with new episodes dropping weekly on Fridays at midnight PT.

articles.title: The Surprise Guest in ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win an Oscar. Should They?
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters. The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried, the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can…
body: To be clear, the parts of “You Can See Everything” when she is literally acting are riveting on their own terms. Seyfried simply wears the role of Holmes easily. She’s doubly disadvantaged — in that we’ve just spent 90 minutes with the real Holmes, against whom we can compare Seyfried, and in that we’ve also spent time absorbing just how little Seyfried understands the enigma of Holmes’ motivations. And yet Seyfried somehow creates a coherent and compelling version of a woman we don’t understand, and we know she doesn’t, really, either.

To pigeonhole Seyfried’s appearance in “You Can See Everything” as, solely, an acting performance misses the rawness of Seyfried’s presence here. She allows herself to be seen thinking through a conundrum, as herself, and falling short of finding answers — in other words, after Holmes and husband Billy Evans, she’s the documentary’s other subject. Seyfried delivers a painful and unresolved excavation of the mind of an actor, seeming to land in a place of uncertainty as to how her own past work as Holmes has changed the story even as she willingly takes on the part once more.

articles.title: New York’s AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says ‘AMC Wants to Stay’ but NYU Langone ‘Wants Us Gone’
articles.summary: AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3. Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with
body: On Aug. 24, Variety reported that the Kips Bay theater would close at the end of 2026, ending a 27-year run at the location. AMC took over the theater in 2006, which became the chain’s second-largest multiplex in the city (after Times Square’s Empire 25 theater). The Kips Bay location has become adored by local residents, who staged a protest in September in an attempt to stop the closure.

“Every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15,” Aron wrote. “It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theaters across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theaters operated by AMC nationally.”

The theater closure comes after a r ecord-breaking summer box office, which saw movies like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and more collectively gross $4.67 billion domestically. There are also major upcoming movies like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III,” which Kips Bay residents will now still get a chance to see at their beloved theater before it closes for good.

articles.title: Box Office: ‘Clayface’ Lands at No. 1 with $10.4 Million Debut, ‘You Can See Everything’ Adds $6.14 Million on Friday
articles.summary: Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from showing out to catch the Batman supervillain’s gory, nightmare-inducing origin story at the box office this weekend.
body: Fellow DC films like “Superman,” produced for nearly $230 million, brought in $618.72 million worldwide over the course of its 2025 theatrical run, while “Supergirl” was considered a bomb with $126 million against a $170 million budget earlier this year. In comparison, “Clayface” cost $44 million to produce.

A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” landed in second place on Friday, making $6.14 million from 2,655 North American theaters, up from 855 at opening weekend. The buzzy doc has made $31.7 million domestically so far. Rival estimates suggest the film will gross another $20 million by Sunday.

Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

articles.title: TV stars to marry in chapel home after proposal 'on Welsh soil'
articles.summary: Keith Brymer Jones and Marj Hogarth are to marry in their chapel home in Pwllheli in May 2027.
body: The Great Pottery Throw Down judge Keith Brymer Jones has told how he and his partner are to marry in their north Wales chapel home after he proposed to her "on Welsh soil".
Jones said he and actor Marj Hogarth, who are renovating a Grade II-listed chapel in Pwllheli, were on tour "and I just thought I ought to really propose to her on Welsh soil".
He proposed during their show at the New Theatre in Cardiff, and "the idea is to get married in the main hall some time in May of next year".
The ceramicist also said there were a lot of derelict chapels across Wales and "we need to repurpose these buildings and give them a new lease of life".

articles.title: Star Trek's Denise Crosby Had A Major Change Of Heart About The Franchise [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Denise Crosby, who played multiple characters on Star Trek, tells us what inspired her to better understand the sci-fi franchise years after being in it.
body: One of the many joys of "Star Trek" is that, thanks to the vast and ever-sprawling universe of movies and shows over its 60 years of existence, there's always room for supporting characters to loom incredibly large. Some reach those lofty heights quite organically — the potential for fan-favorites like Andrew Robinson's Elim Garak in "Deep Space Nine" or even Ro Laren (Michelle Forbes) in "The Next Generation" felt apparent almost as soon as they arrived on the scene, for example. But others required a fair amount of time to sink into the "Trek" melting pot, garner enough love and good will among the fanbase, and ultimately end up standing alongside the undisputed pillars of the franchise.

While promoting the new documentary "The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World" at this year's New York Comic Con, Crosby spoke to me about her unconventional journey through "Trek," her legacy, and what finally made her appreciate the fandom's love of Tasha Yar.

articles.title: Clayface Doesn't Need A Sequel Because We've Already Seen What Happens Next
articles.summary: Clayface serves as an origin story that could lead into a sequel - except Matt Hagen's future has already been revealed elsewhere in the DC Universe.
body: The DC Universe has expanded with the release of "Clayface." A full-blown, R-rated horror movie centered on the famed "Batman" villain, it's shaking up the status quo in the realm of comic book adaptations. It's very far removed from the likes of "Superman" and "Supergirl." But is this really a one-off? The "Clayface" ending leaves viewers wondering if Matt Hagen will return. That said, we already know what happens with his story after the events of the movie.

Directed by James Watkins ("Speak No Evil"), the latest movie in the DC Universe centers on Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), chronicling his meteoric rise from Gotham City street kid to Hollywood leading man. It's cut short when a local crime boss leaves him horribly disfigured. Abandoned by his team with nothing left, Matt seeks out a cutting edge treatment that miraculously heals him — or so it seems. The treatment unexpectedly affects his grip on reality, sending him down a destructive path of revenge.

articles.title: Bill Murray Is Generally OK Giving You a “Bill Murray Moment”
articles.summary: "If you're living correctly, it's not a burden," Murray tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of his and Tom Coyne's new Paramount golf/travel series.
body: A Course Called Ireland, an adaptation of Coyne’s 2009 book of the same name, premieres Sunday on Paramount+. The six-episode, 30-minutes-per-episode series is as breezy as the Irish coast’s weather. Its original intention was to retrace the journey chronicled in Coyne’s bestseller — the golf writer once walked the island playing every golf course it had to offer — but this version of A Course Called Ireland became, as Murray grumpily laments in at least one episode to a director, “The Bill Murray Fucking Show.”
Murray has time for pretty much everyone who wants a photo — it is the production crew taking the professional videos he’d like to avert the lenses of.

“I’m heavy in the show. For an executive producer, that’s about as heavy as you can get,” Murray told The Hollywood Reporter. “I don’t want to complain about that. I did my complaining then. It’s too late to complain.”

I’m on a Zoom call with Murray, who is wandering the streets of Boston solo after sunset, and Coyne, who is sitting in a house in the Carribean. In a bucket hat and without a care in the world, Murray speaks kindly but candidly about making his buddy Coyne’s TV dream come true.

articles.title: Ryan Gosling's Star Wars Movie May Have A Bigger Budget Than The Force Awakens
articles.summary: Star Wars: Starfighter is shaping up to be quite pricey, with the Ryan Gosling-led movie having cost more during filming than The Force Awakens.
body: According to Forbes, Shawn Levy's upcoming film "Star Wars: Starfighter," which is being fronted by Ryan Gosling, had already cost $226.5 million to make by the time filming was done. For context, that's more than J.J. Abram's 2015 ultra-blockbuster "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens" cost at the same point in its development. Indeed, in 2025, a separate Forbes report revealed that "The Force Awakens" had a total budget of $638.9 million prior to accounting for tax credits, making it one of the most expensive movies of all time.

Of course, it's worth remembering that "The Force Awakens" remains Disney's most profitable "Star Wars" movie to date, with earnings of $500.2 million thanks to its gargantuan box office haul. No doubt, that's part of why Mouse House is willing to risk spending a similar amount to make "Star Wars: Starfighter." For the time being, though, it remains to be how much post-production on the movie winds up costing.

articles.title: Jay-Z’s Victory Lap Continues as He Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, John Legend, DJ Khaled for SoFi Stadium Opening Night
articles.summary: The rapper also brought out Scarface as a special guest for the first of two much anticipated L.A. shows on Friday night.
body: “I’ve been away too long,” Jay-Z told a hyped-up SoFi Stadium crowd soon after taking the stage on Friday night. The rap icon was met with cheers as he, at last, brought his yearlong victory tour to Los Angeles.

The result was a career-spanning tour de force from one of hip-hop’s most seminal figures, and perhaps more Yankee hats and jerseys in the crowd than SoFi Stadium has ever seen. Kicking off just before 9:30 p.m. local time, the show opened with a video of Jay and Beyoncé alone in the seats at Yankee Stadium, with Bey behind him playing with her husband’s hair.

Flanked by an impressive backing band and starting the night with “Hovi Baby,” Jay powered through a collection of hits and fan favorites for two hours, from “FuckWithMeYouKnowIGotIt” to “Run This Town,” “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “Lucifer” and “99 Problems.”
“Let me take you back to my home for a second,” Jay told the crowd before launching into “Empire State of Mind” toward the end of the evening.

articles.title: Online Comedians Are Making a Mint Mocking Wall Street
articles.summary: Hedge fund jerks and private equity bros are being pilloried by popular creator comedians — and the finance world is laughing along.
body: Johnny Hilbrant Partridge never worked an hour on Wall Street, but you’d never guess that by looking at him. Nearly every day, Partridge takes to YouTube to channel his inner finance bro as P.E. Guy, a puffer-vested private equity putz who brags about his million-dollar deals, Aspen manse and private plane.

Although Partridge lampoons private equity, his skits resonate beyond buyout boys. “I think a lot of people have that experience of coming in contact with somebody who wants to one-up you and make you feel like they win the conversation because they have an impressive-sounding job,” he says.

As certain business figures become as talked about as celebrities, Wall Street yuksters like Partridge are surging on social media. While memes still flood finance bro DMs, creator-helmed videos are gaining momentum on both Wall Street and Main Street. Some riff on Bloomberg headlines, while others simply play on C-suite stereotypes.
